title: Volumes & Bind Mounts
summary: Why container files vanish, and how volumes, bind mounts and tmpfs mounts keep or share data.

sections.heading: The writable layer and mount types

blocks.text: Files a container creates land in a **writable container layer** on top of the read-only image layers. That layer is unique to the container and is **lost when the container is destroyed**, and it's hard to get data out of it.

rows: Host filesystem, managed by the Docker daemon
Long-term and performance-critical data; survives container removal
Files both the host and the container must access
Temporary data such as caches or credentials; gone on stop or restart

items: Image mounts and named pipes also exist. Image mounts need the containerd image store.
Whatever the type, the container just sees a directory or a file.
Don't touch volume data on the host directly; that is unsupported and can break the volume.

blocks.text: A volume outlives any single container. Mount the same volume into a new container and the files are still there.

docker volume create log-data
docker run -d -p 80:80 -v log-data:/logs docker/welcome-to-docker

# database example: recreate the container, keep the data
docker run --name=db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -d -v postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql postgres:18
docker stop db && docker rm db
docker run --name=new-db -d -v postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql postgres:18

items: If the named volume doesn't exist, `docker run -v` creates it.
One volume can be attached to several containers to share files.
`docker volume ls` lists volumes; `docker volume rm <name>` removes one that no container is using; `docker volume prune` removes all unused volumes.

blocks.text: `docker volume rm` fails while a container still uses the volume. Remove the container first, e.g. `docker rm -f <container>` (stops it, then removes it).

items: Volumes are the **preferred** way to persist container data: easier to back up and migrate than bind mounts, managed with the Docker CLI or API, work on Linux and Windows containers, safer to share, and good for high-performance I/O.
They don't grow the container's size, and they're faster than writing to the writable layer, which goes through a storage driver.
They're a poor fit when the host needs to access the files; use a bind mount then.
A volume isn't removed automatically when no container uses it.

rows: Empty volume over a non-empty directory
The directory's files are copied into the volume (disable with `volume-nocopy`)
Non-empty volume over a non-empty directory
Existing files are hidden by the mount
Random unique name; each container gets its own; kept after container removal unless `--rm` was used

blocks.text:
docker run --mount type=volume,src=<volume-name>,dst=<mount-path> <image>
docker run -v <volume-name>:<mount-path> <image>

# read-only
docker run -d --name=nginxtest --mount source=nginx-vol,destination=/usr/share/nginx/html,readonly nginx:latest
docker run -d --name=nginxtest -v nginx-vol:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro nginx:latest

items: `-v` has three colon-separated fields in fixed order: `[<volume-name>:]<mount-path>[:opts]`. Omit the name for an anonymous volume.
`--mount` takes comma-separated `key=value` pairs in any order: `source`/`src`, `destination`/`dst`/`target`, `readonly`/`ro`, `volume-nocopy`, `volume-subpath`, `volume-opt`.
`--mount` is generally preferred. You **must** use it for volume driver options, a volume subdirectory, or Swarm services.

blocks.text:
docker volume create my-vol
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect my-vol   # Driver local, Mountpoint /var/lib/docker/volumes/my-vol/_data
docker volume rm my-vol
docker volume prune            # all unused volumes
Check a mount with `docker inspect <container>` and read the `Mounts` section: `Type`, `Source`, `Destination` and `RW` (false when read-only).

A bind mount puts a host file or directory into the container. Typical uses: sharing source code or build output in development, writing files back to the host, and sharing config files (Docker mounts the host's `/etc/resolv.conf` this way for DNS).

docker run -d -it --name devtest --mount type=bind,source="$(pwd)"/target,target=/app nginx:latest
docker run -d -it --name devtest -v "$(pwd)"/target:/app nginx:latest
docker run -d -it --name devtest -v "$(pwd)"/target:/app:ro nginx:latest   # read-only

rows: Docker creates it on the host, always as a directory
Error: bind source path does not exist (unless you add `bind-create-src`)

items: Bind mounts are **writable by default**, so container processes can change or delete host files. Add `ro`/`readonly` to prevent that.
The path is on the **daemon** host, not the client, and the container depends on that host's directory layout.
Mounting over a non-empty container directory hides its contents. Unlike volumes, nothing is copied.
SELinux `z`/`Z` labeling is listed among the `-v` options, not the `--mount` options. It relabels the host path itself, so use it with great care.
Data the container creates or changes and must keep after it stops → **volume**.
Specific host files you want the container to see directly, like config or code under development → **bind mount**.
Append `:ro` (read-only) or `:rw` (read-write) to control access. Read-only stops the container changing or deleting host files; read-write changes appear on the host.

blocks.text:
docker run -v /HOST/PATH:/CONTAINER/PATH -it nginx
docker run --mount type=bind,source=/HOST/PATH,target=/CONTAINER/PATH,readonly nginx
Docker recommends `--mount` over `-v`: it gives more control and errors on a missing host path instead of silently creating a directory.

docker run -d --tmpfs /run:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=65536k <image>
docker run --read-only -v /icanwrite busybox touch /icanwrite/here
docker run --rm -v /foo -v awesome:/bar busybox top

items: `--tmpfs` creates a tmpfs mount; its options match Linux `mount -t tmpfs -o`.
`--read-only` makes the container's root filesystem read-only, so it can write only to the volumes you give it.
`--rm` removes the container's **anonymous** volumes too. In the last example `/foo` is removed but the named volume `awesome` is kept.

flashcards.front: What happens to data in a container's writable layer when the container is destroyed?
flashcards.back: It's lost. The writable layer is unique to the container and doesn't persist.

flashcards.front: Where does a tmpfs mount store data?
flashcards.back: In host memory only, never on disk. It's gone when the container stops or restarts.

flashcards.front: Command to remove all unused volumes?
When does docker volume rm work?
flashcards.back: Only when no container is using the volume.

flashcards.front: What happens when an empty volume is mounted over a container directory that has files?
flashcards.back: The files are copied into the volume, unless volume-nocopy is set.

flashcards.front: Three cases where you must use --mount rather than -v for volumes?
flashcards.back: Volume driver options, mounting a volume subdirectory, and Swarm services.

flashcards.front: Default Mountpoint shown by docker volume inspect my-vol?
-v vs --mount when the bind-mount host path doesn't exist?
flashcards.back: -v creates a directory on the host; --mount errors unless bind-create-src is set.

flashcards.front: Are bind mounts read-only or writable by default?
flashcards.back: Writable. Add ro / readonly to prevent writes.

flashcards.front: Volume or bind mount for code you edit on the host and want live in the container?
flashcards.back: Bind mount. Use a volume for data the container produces and must keep.

flashcards.front: Which volumes does docker run --rm delete on exit?
flashcards.back: Anonymous volumes only. Named volumes are kept.
Mounts the container's root filesystem read-only; it can still write to its volumes.

questions.stem: You remove a database container that stored its data only in its writable layer. What happens to the data?

options.text: It is lost with the container
options.explanation: Writable-layer data doesn't persist when the container is destroyed.

options.text: It moves to an anonymous volume
options.explanation: Nothing is moved automatically; the layer is discarded.

options.text: It is saved into the image
options.explanation: Image layers are read-only and immutable.

options.text: It remains in a tmpfs mount
options.explanation: tmpfs is memory-only and is also lost when the container stops.

questions.stem: An app needs scratch space for sensitive temporary data that must never hit disk. Which mount fits?

options.explanation: Stored in host memory only and not persisted.
Volumes store data on the host filesystem.
Bind mounts write to a host path on disk.
Image mounts are read-only content from another image.

questions.stem: docker run -v log-data:/logs <image> fails if the volume log-data hasn't been created yet.

options.explanation: Docker creates the missing volume automatically.
The volume is created for you.

questions.stem: docker volume rm postgres_data fails because the volume is in use. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the container using it (e.g. docker rm -f <container>), then remove the volume
options.explanation: A volume can only be removed when no container is attached.
ls only lists volumes; it doesn't detach anything.
That creates a volume, not removes one.
prune removes only unused volumes, so an attached one stays.

questions.stem: Which are reasons the Docker docs give for preferring volumes over bind mounts? Select 3.

options.text: Easier to back up or migrate
options.explanation: Listed as a volume advantage.

options.text: Manageable with Docker CLI commands or the Docker API
options.explanation: Listed as a volume advantage.

options.text: Work on both Linux and Windows containers
options.explanation: Listed as a volume advantage.

options.text: Easy to edit directly from the host
options.explanation: Volumes are a poor choice when the host needs the files; use a bind mount.

questions.stem: You start nginx with a new, empty volume mounted at /usr/share/nginx/html. What ends up in the volume?

options.text: nginx's default HTML files, copied from the container directory
options.explanation: Files in the target directory are copied into an empty volume by default.
That happens only with volume-nocopy.

options.text: The files are hidden and the volume stays empty
options.explanation: Hiding happens when a non-empty volume is mounted over existing files.
This is the documented way to pre-populate a volume.

questions.stem: Which command mounts the volume nginx-vol read-only at /usr/share/nginx/html?

options.explanation: ro in the third -v field makes it read-only.
Without readonly (or ro) the volume is mounted read-write.
-v fields are in fixed order: name, path, options.
volume-nocopy stops copying into an empty volume; it doesn't make it read-only.

questions.stem: For volumes, which require --mount rather than -v? Select 2.

options.explanation: Only --mount supports volume-subpath.
Driver options need --mount.
-v supports ro too.
-v <volume-name>:<mount-path> works.

questions.stem: docker run --mount type=bind,src=/dev/noexist,dst=/mnt/foo alpine returns an error. Why?

options.text: --mount doesn't create a missing host path by default
options.explanation: Add bind-create-src or create the directory first.
Both --mount and -v create bind mounts.

options.text: dst must be a relative path
options.explanation: The container path must be absolute.

options.text: alpine images can't use bind mounts
options.explanation: The image isn't the problem; the source path is missing.

questions.stem: A process in a container can modify host files through a bind mount unless it's mounted read-only.

options.explanation: Bind mounts are writable by default; use ro to block writes.
Write access is the default for bind mounts.

questions.stem: You bind-mount a host directory over a non-empty directory in the container. What happens to the container's original files?

options.text: They are hidden by the mount
options.explanation: Pre-existing files are obscured; recreate the container without the mount to see them.

options.text: They are copied to the host directory
options.explanation: Copying into an empty mount is volume behaviour, not bind-mount behaviour.

options.text: They are merged with the host files
options.explanation: No merge happens; the mount replaces the view.
The mount succeeds; the files are just hidden.

questions.stem: You want the container to always see your latest build output from the host. Which storage option fits?

options.explanation: Bind mounts share specific host files directly; ideal for development.
Volumes are for data the container generates and must keep.

options.text: Copying the files into the image
options.explanation: Files baked into the image don't follow later changes on the host; a bind mount shares the host files directly.
By default a container can't directly access data on the host; you need a bind mount or volume for that.

questions.stem: docker run --rm -v /foo -v awesome:/bar busybox top exits. Which volumes remain?

options.explanation: --rm removes anonymous volumes (/foo) but keeps named ones.
The anonymous /foo volume is removed with the container.
Named volumes survive --rm.
It's the other way round.

questions.stem: You run a container with --read-only and it must still write files under /icanwrite. What do you add?

options.explanation: With a read-only root, writes go only to the volumes you specify.
That grants extended privileges, not a writable path.
-w sets the working directory only.
:ro mounts read-only.
